title: Carnitas Tacos
subtitle: Slow-cooked pulled pork shoulder, crispy-edged in the pan
excerpt: Pork shoulder braised low and slow with orange, garlic, and cumin until it falls apart, then crisped in its own fat and served in warm corn tortillas. The braise takes 3 hours; the result is worth every minute.
sourceNotes: Carnitas: a classic Mexican dish of slow-braised then pan-crisped pork, widely adopted into Tex-Mex cooking. Traditional preparation from Michoacán state; Tex-Mex adaptations use orange juice and common spices. Drawn from classic Tex-Mex home-cooking sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: The cooked pulled pork (before crisping) freezes well for up to 3 months. Defrost, then crisp in a hot pan.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch of the braised pork; crisp portions to order as needed.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Braise the pork up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate in its cooking liquid. Crisp in a hot pan to serve.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Mexican preparation of pork slowly braised in its own fat until tender, then crisped in a hot pan. The name means 'little meats' in Spanish.

content.text: are pork shoulder braised slowly until it falls apart, then crisped in a hot pan so the edges catch and brown. The contrast between the tender pulled interior and the caramelised outer pieces is what makes these tacos. Allow 3 hours for the braise; the hands-on time is under 20 minutes.
A casserole dish (Dutch oven) with a lid is ideal for the oven braise. A cast-iron skillet gets the best crisping result at the end.
Heat the oven to 160°C. Season the pork chunks all over with salt, the cumin, chilli powder, and oregano.
Heat the vegetable oil in a casserole dish over high heat. Sear the pork on all sides until golden brown, about 3-4 minutes per side. Work in batches if needed.
Return all the pork to the casserole. Add the crushed garlic, bay leaves, orange juice, and lime juice. Add enough water to come halfway up the pork, about 200 ml.
Cover and cook in the oven at 160°C for 2.5-3 hours until the pork is completely tender and pulls apart with a fork. Check halfway through and add a splash of water if the pot looks dry.
Remove the pork from the liquid. Shred roughly with two forks; you want some larger pieces alongside the pulled shreds.

Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of oil. Spread the shredded pork in the pan and press it down lightly. Leave untouched for 3-4 minutes until the underside crisps and caramelises. Toss briefly and serve.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. Set out coriander, diced red onion, avocado, lime wedges, and jalapeño. Fill and eat straight away.

items.cause: Not cooked long enough, or the liquid boiled rather than simmered
items.fix: Pork shoulder needs low, slow heat to break down the connective tissue. Check at 2.5 hours; it may need the full 3 hours. The pot should barely tremble, not boil.

items.symptom: Carnitas won't crisp in the pan
items.cause: Pork too wet, or pan not hot enough
items.fix: Pat the shredded pork dry before adding to the pan. The pan needs to be properly hot before the meat goes in. Don't stir; leave it to form a crust.

items.symptom: Dry and stringy rather than tender
items.cause: Lean pork shoulder used, or braised without enough liquid
items.fix: Pork shoulder needs some fat to braise properly. Don't trim it too lean. Make sure the liquid reaches halfway up the meat.

items.cause: Not enough salt, or spices not given time to penetrate
items.fix: Season generously before searing. The orange and lime juice should taste bright in the braising liquid; add more if the liquid smells flat.

content.text: The braised pork keeps refrigerated in its cooking liquid for 3 days. Reheat with a splash of the liquid in a covered pan before crisping. Freezes well for up to 3 months; defrost overnight and proceed from the crisping step.

Carnitas come from Michoacán in central Mexico, where pork slow-cooked in its own fat has been made for centuries. The Tex-Mex version uses oven heat and citrus juice instead of the traditional lard submersion, but keeps the key finish: high heat for crisp edges and a tender centre. In Mexico City, street vendors pile carnitas into corn tortillas with just onion and coriander. The simplicity is the point.
